items.title: The Elizabethan Settlement (1559) was a deliberate compromise
items.claim: What did the Elizabethan Religious Settlement of 1559 establish?

options.text: Act of Supremacy (Elizabeth as 'Supreme Governor' — softer than 'Supreme Head'); Act of Uniformity (revised 1559 Prayer Book); Thirty-Nine Articles (1571 final) — a deliberately broad 'via media' between Catholic and Reformed

items.reveal:
Elizabeth's first Parliament (1559) produced the legislation by narrow margins — particularly the Act of Supremacy, opposed by all 18 surviving bishops from Mary's reign. The 1559 Prayer Book combined elements of Cranmer's 1549 and 1552 books, with deliberately ambiguous language on the Eucharist.

The Act of Uniformity required attendance at parish church on pain of fines. The Thirty-Nine Articles (1563, finalised 1571) defined Anglican doctrine. The Settlement was challenged by Puritans wanting further reform and by Catholic recusants.

Elizabeth reportedly said she would not 'open windows into men's souls' — outward conformity was required; private belief was largely left alone.
items.why: The Church of England's modern shape — episcopal, vernacular, broad — is a 1559 political compromise that became national habit over 45 years. One of the most successful exercises in deliberate ambiguity in European history.

items.title: The First Crusade captured Jerusalem with massacre in 1099
items.claim: What happened when the First Crusade took Jerusalem?

options.text: On 15 July 1099 crusaders breached the walls; over the following days a massacre of Muslim and Jewish inhabitants followed — chroniclers (including Raymond of Aguilers) recorded slaughter so extensive that 'one waded in blood up to the ankles'

items.reveal:
The crusade had left Europe in 1096. After taking Antioch (1098), the army of around 14,000 reached Jerusalem in June 1099. The walls were breached on 15 July; the massacre that followed killed thousands. Jewish inhabitants who took refuge in a synagogue were burned alive.

Godfrey of Bouillon was elected 'Defender of the Holy Sepulchre' (refusing the title of king); his brother Baldwin became Baldwin I of Jerusalem in 1100. The Kingdom of Jerusalem lasted until 1291 (fall of Acre).

Saladin recaptured Jerusalem in 1187 with notably less violence — he allowed inhabitants to ransom themselves and many to leave safely, in deliberate contrast to 1099.
items.why: Religious warfare in the high Middle Ages was often atrocious. The 1099 massacre shaped Muslim-Christian relations for centuries — and the comparison with Saladin's 1187 conduct is one that Muslim sources have made repeatedly.

items.title: Most Roman emperors died violently
items.claim: Of the 69 Roman emperors from Augustus (27 BCE) to Theodosius I (395 CE), how many died of natural causes?

options.text: Almost all — emperors were generally well-protected
Roughly a third — the rest died by assassination, in battle, by suicide or under suspicious circumstances
All emperors after Nero were murdered

items.reveal:
Joseph Saleh and colleagues (2019) modelled imperial deaths and found violent end rates above 50% for the first 25 years of any reign. The Crisis of the Third Century (235-284) saw around 50 emperors and usurpers in 50 years.

Named assassinations: Caligula (41), Claudius (54, probably poisoned by Agrippina), Domitian (96), Commodus (192), Caracalla (217), Elagabalus (222) and many more. Some died in war (Decius at Abrittus, 251; Valerian captured by the Persians, 260).
items.why: The imperial succession looks orderly from the list of names. Statistically, becoming emperor was one of the most dangerous jobs in the ancient world — which itself shaped imperial policy.
